planting.note: Repot or divide in spring into a coarse, well-drained terrestrial orchid mix, giving roots room since this species forms a substantial clump over years.

directions: Native to the forest floors and humus-rich slopes of Vietnam, Thailand, and surrounding Indochina, this terrestrial to semi-terrestrial species sends up tall, upright to slightly arching spikes carrying a dozen or more waxy, pale pink to near-white flowers lightly spotted at the lip in winter. It is historically important as a breeding parent, standing behind the primary hybrid Cymbidium eburneo-lowianum, which was crossed with this species to raise the foundational grex Cymbidium Alexanderi and, through its spontaneous 'Westonbirt' tetraploid, much of the large-flowered cymbidium breeding grown commercially today. Grow in bright, filtered light with a distinct cool, dry snap in autumn to trigger spiking, watering generously through active growth and easing off once flower spikes appear. Repot only every two to three years in a coarse terrestrial mix, since cymbidiums flower best when slightly pot-bound.

planting.note: Mount or pot in a coarse bark mix in spring, giving the tall canes a stake or support until roots anchor them.

directions: Native to the coastal Atlantic forest of Brazil, this tall, slender-caned Cattleya produces clustered sprays of waxy yellow-green flowers heavily spotted and barred in maroon-brown, set off by a contrasting rose-purple lip, opening in fall on mature pseudobulbs. Its cluster-type inflorescence and bold spotted color pattern have made it a frequently used parent in breeding dark, patterned Cattleya-alliance hybrids, including the cultivar Chocolate Drop. Grow under standard Cattleya conditions, in bright, filtered light with strong air movement and a coarse, fast-draining bark mix, watering thoroughly and letting the medium approach dryness between waterings. Give it a brief, cooler, drier rest once each new growth matures to encourage a reliable flowering cycle the following season.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot in a small, coarse bark mix in spring; this species tolerates more light and less pampering than most Cattleya relatives.

directions: Native from Mexico south through Central America to Panama, this compact, free-flowering species (long sold as Cattleya aurantiaca) bears dense clusters of small, waxy, tubular orange to orange-red flowers that stay only partly open, carried on a tough, sun-tolerant plant that handles brighter light and less humidity than most of its Cattleya-alliance relatives. It has been widely used as a breeding parent to introduce orange and red tones and cluster-type flowering into modern Cattleya-alliance hybrids, including the cultivar Chocolate Drop. Grow in bright light with good air movement in a small, coarse bark mix, watering thoroughly through active growth and allowing the mix to dry between waterings. Its compact size and easy nature make it a forgiving introduction to warm-growing Cattleya-type culture.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring as a flat, spreading groundcover on a slope, bank, or foundation bed in full sun.

directions: Youngstown is an older, widely planted selection of creeping juniper valued for its bright, consistent mid-green foliage and flat, fast-spreading habit, long used in municipal, highway, and residential landscaping as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover for slopes and banks. It tolerates poor, dry, and alkaline soils with ease once established and resists the straggly, open center that develops in some older creeping juniper selections. Its stable, true-green color and vigorous growth have also made it useful breeding stock, standing as the parent from which the golden-foliaged sport 'Lime Glow' arose. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage, and avoid heavy, consistently wet soils that encourage root and crown rot.
